claims.text: McDonald testified before the House Committee on Science and Astronautics on 29 July 1968 as senior physicist at the University of Arizona Institute of Atmospheric Physics.

McDonald told the committee that 'credible observers are observing relatively incredible objects' and argued the phenomenon deserved serious scientific investigation rather than dismissal through ridicule.

claims.source: McDonald's 1968 testimony and contemporaneous papers to scientific societies
claims.text: McDonald concluded after reviewing Blue Book case files that the program was not conducting genuine scientific investigation.

claims.source: Inference from the hearing record and the coroner's finding
claims.text: The 1971 SST hearing ridicule and McDonald's death three months later form the earliest instance of the reputational-destruction pattern that recurs through the disclosure record; no causal claim beyond the documented sequence is asserted.

The Condon Report acknowledges McDonald directly: 'The help of Dr. McDonald, Institute for Atmospheric Physics, University of Arizona, who conducted a study of UFO phenomena concurrently with this study, was invaluable in bringing a number of cases to our attention.' The board's description of him as a senior atmospheric physicist is the project's own.

The report records that 'in August 1967 Prof. James McDonald of Arizona made a 20-day trip to Australia, Tasmania and New Zealand in the course of which he interviewed some 80 persons who had made UFO reports there', and that on his return he briefed the Colorado project on what he found.

McDonald is indexed in the Condon Report at pages 927 and 928, and separately for his part in Case 50 (657-662), Case 52 (683-684, 690, 692), his views on future research (1269), the northeast power outage (167) and the extraterrestrial hypothesis (34). He is the most heavily indexed outside critic in the study that was meant to close the question.

label: James E. McDonald
narrative: James E. McDonald was a senior atmospheric physicist at the University of Arizona and the most aggressive scientific critic the Air Force UFO program ever faced. He obtained access to Blue Book files, re-investigated cases himself, and concluded the program was not an investigation at all. On 29 July 1968 he testified to the House Committee on Science and Astronautics, telling Congress that 'credible observers are observing relatively incredible objects' and that the phenomenon warranted serious scientific attention rather than dismissal by ridicule. He was the conduit through which the Low memo reached the press, and he attacked the Condon Report publicly after its release. McDonald was subsequently humiliated in a 1971 congressional hearing on the SST — an unrelated subject on which he was a technical critic — when a member used his UFO interest to discredit him from the dais. He shot himself in the Arizona desert on 13 June 1971. His death is the earliest entry in the pattern this board tracks of scientific and official careers destroyed on this subject, and it is recorded here as such without any implication beyond the documented sequence.
